words.definition: Agreement or harmony among parts, opinions, or sounds within a whole.
words.example: The consonance between the couple's core values made their partnership feel effortless.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + sonance (sound) — sounds sounding together in harmony.

words.definition: In agreement with or fitting the character of something else.
words.example: Her minimalist decor was consonant with the calm, unhurried way she lived.
words.mnemonic: Picture two 'sonants' (sounds) that fit together — ideas that go hand in hand.

words.definition: A state of agreement between things; also an alphabetical index of a text's words.
words.example: The concordance between the two witnesses' accounts convinced the jury on the spot.
words.mnemonic: con- (with) + cord (Latin 'cor', heart) — hearts beating together, in agreement.

words.definition: The quality of being in harmony or of parts suiting one another well.
words.example: There was a pleasing congruity between the somber music and the film's grief.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'con-GREE-ity' — the state where things con-GREE (agree).

words.definition: Corresponding or fitting well together; matching in a consistent way.
words.example: People trusted him because his actions were always congruent with his promises.
words.mnemonic: In geometry, congruent triangles match exactly — congruent things line up perfectly.

words.definition: A lack of harmony, or the quality of being out of place or mismatched.
words.example: The incongruity of a tuxedo at the muddy beach picnic made everyone laugh.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + congruity — the flat opposite of things fitting together.

words.definition: To bring into agreement or make separate elements blend pleasingly.
words.example: The mediator worked to harmonize the clashing demands of the two departments.
words.mnemonic: Singers harmonize — different voices blend into one pleasing sound.

words.definition: To adjust or bring into a responsive, receptive relationship with something.
words.example: Years in the classroom had attuned her to the faintest signs of a struggling child.
words.mnemonic: a-TUNE — like tuning an instrument until it matches the right pitch.

words.definition: The state of acting or sounding together at the same moment in agreement.
words.example: The crowd shouted the final countdown in unison as the ball began to drop.
words.mnemonic: uni- (one) + son (sound) — one single sound made all together.

words.definition: Complete agreement among everyone in a group about a matter.
words.example: The rare unanimity of the fractious committee meant the proposal passed instantly.
words.mnemonic: uni- (one) + anim (Latin 'animus', mind) — everyone sharing one mind.

words.definition: Agreed to or shared by every single member of a group.
words.example: The jury returned a unanimous verdict, leaving no room for doubt.
words.mnemonic: uni- (one) + anim (mind) — all of one mind, not a single dissenter.

words.definition: The restoring of friendly relations and harmony after a quarrel or dispute.
words.example: After years of icy silence, the brothers finally met for a tearful reconciliation.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + concili- (council, coming together) — returning to the same table.

words.definition: Intended to soothe anger, win goodwill, or ease a dispute.
words.example: He offered a conciliatory smile and a quiet apology to calm the tense room.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'reconcile' inside it — a conciliatory gesture reconciles enemies.

words.definition: An easing of tension or hostility, especially between rival nations.
words.example: The two superpowers reached a détente after decades of nuclear brinkmanship.
words.mnemonic: French 'détente' means relaxing a drawn spring or trigger — tension released.

words.definition: Courteous, respectful conduct and mutual recognition between people or nations.
words.example: A spirit of comity let the rival senators debate fiercely without personal insults.
words.mnemonic: Think 'come-unity' — coming together with courtesy and friendly relations.

words.definition: Marked by friendliness and the absence of conflict between people.
words.example: Despite the divorce, they reached an amicable settlement and still share holidays together.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'amic-', from Spanish 'amigo' (friend) — amicable people act like old amigos.

words.definition: The quality of being pleasant, warm, and easy to approach in conversation.
words.example: The host's affability put even the shyest guests at ease within minutes.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'a-FAB-ility' — the ability to be fab and chatty, so people love talking to you.

words.definition: Warm, sincere, and polite in the way one treats others.
words.example: They exchanged a cordial handshake before sitting down to negotiate the deal.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'cor' means heart (as in 'core'); a cordial greeting comes straight from the heart — also a sweet, warming drink.

words.definition: Cheerful, kindly, and pleasant in disposition.
words.example: The genial innkeeper greeted every traveler with a joke and a hot bowl of soup.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'genie' — picture a smiling, good-natured genie popping out to spread cheer.

words.definition: A spirit of trust and friendship shared among a group of companions.
words.example: After weeks in the trenches, a deep camaraderie bound the soldiers to one another.
words.mnemonic: It literally contains 'comrade' — the warm bond you feel among your comrades.

words.definition: A close relationship in which people understand each other and communicate easily.
words.example: The therapist quickly built a rapport with the nervous teenager, who soon opened up.
words.mnemonic: Say 'rah-POR' — imagine two people 'reporting' thoughts back and forth, perfectly in sync.

words.definition: Unity and mutual support among people sharing a common interest or goal.
words.example: Workers across the city walked out in solidarity with the striking nurses.
words.mnemonic: It starts with 'solid' — a group standing solid and unbroken behind one another.

words.definition: The state of sticking together and acting as one unified whole.
words.example: The new coach restored team cohesion, and they finally played as a single unit.
words.mnemonic: 'Co-' (together) + the idea of 'adhesion' (sticking) — parts sticking firmly together.

words.definition: To blend or merge two or more things into a single whole.
words.example: The chef melds sweet and spicy notes into one unforgettable sauce.
words.mnemonic: 'Meld' = 'melt' + 'weld' — things melt down and weld into one.

words.definition: To mix or combine two or more things so they are no longer separate.
words.example: The bank was accused of commingling client money with its own corporate accounts.
words.mnemonic: 'Com-' (together) + 'mingle' — guests mingling together at a party until the groups blend.

words.definition: A close relationship between two different parties that benefits both.
words.example: The clownfish and the anemone live in perfect symbiosis, each sheltering the other.
words.mnemonic: 'Sym-' (together) + 'bio' (life) — two lives living together for mutual gain.

words.definition: The extra benefit gained when people or things work together effectively.
words.example: The merger created real synergy: the two firms sold far more combined than apart.
words.mnemonic: 'Syn-' (together) + 'ergy' (energy/work) — combined energy producing more than the parts.

words.definition: To socialize or be on friendly terms with others, often against the rules.
words.example: Officers were forbidden to fraternize with enlisted troops while off duty.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'frater' = brother (think 'fraternity') — to buddy up and treat someone like a brother.

words.definition: Able to exist or function together without conflict.
words.example: The old printer isn't compatible with the new laptop, so the driver refuses to install.
words.mnemonic: 'Com-' (together) + 'pati' (to feel, as in sympathy) — feeling well together, getting along.

words.definition: Eager to please others by readily agreeing or going along with them.
words.example: The complaisant waiter honored every odd request without a flicker of protest.
words.mnemonic: From French 'plaire' (to please) — a complaisant person aims to please; don't confuse it with 'complacent' (smugly self-satisfied).

words.definition: In agreement or harmony with something else; consistent and matching.
words.example: The witness's story was fully accordant with the security footage, so the detective closed the case.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a chord' — notes in a chord blend in harmony, and accordant things fit together the same way.

words.definition: Conflict or tension arising between people who disagree.
words.example: There was constant friction between the two managers, and every meeting ended in raised voices.
words.mnemonic: Rub two surfaces and you get heat — rub two personalities and you get friction.

words.definition: A small dissenting group within a larger body, often at odds with the rest.
words.example: A breakaway faction of the party refused to back the leader and started drafting its own manifesto.
words.mnemonic: A 'fraction' of a group splits off to form a faction — drop the 'r' and you have a splinter cell.

words.definition: Inclined to create division or dissent within a group.
words.example: The committee grew so factious that members split into rival camps and stopped speaking to one another.
words.mnemonic: Faction + -ous = full of factions; a factious mood is one that keeps breeding little warring groups.

words.definition: Heated disagreement or dispute between opposing sides.
words.example: The border remained a point of contention, and neither government would concede an inch of it.
words.mnemonic: Think 'con-tension' — two sides pulling with tension against each other create contention.

words.definition: To argue about petty, unimportant matters.
words.example: The children bickered over who got the window seat until their mother threatened to turn the car around.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pecker' — imagine two hens pecking and squabbling over crumbs, that petty snapping is to bicker.

words.definition: A prolonged, bitter feud driven by a desire for revenge.
words.example: After his brother was killed, the man pursued a lifelong vendetta against the rival clan.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'vendetta' (vengeance) — picture a masked avenger 'vending' payback across generations.

words.definition: Active opposition or deep-seated hostility between people or forces.
words.example: There was open antagonism between the two coaches, and they refused to shake hands after the match.
words.mnemonic: The 'antagonist' is the villain who opposes the hero — antagonism is that force of opposition itself.

words.definition: Full of bitter, long-lasting resentment or ill will.
words.example: The divorce turned rancorous, with each spouse leaking damaging secrets to mutual friends.
words.mnemonic: 'Rancid' milk goes sour and bitter — a rancorous person is soured by bitterness that won't fade.

words.definition: Unfriendly, aggressive feelings or behavior toward another.
words.example: The new employee sensed the team's hostility the moment nobody offered her a seat.
words.mnemonic: A 'hostile' army treats you as an enemy — hostility is that enemy-toward-you attitude.

words.definition: An eager, aggressive readiness to fight or start conflict.
words.example: His belligerence at the bar cleared the room, as he squared up to anyone who glanced his way.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'bellum' = war (as in 'rebel'); belligerence is a bellowing eagerness to wage war.

words.definition: Prone to arguing and starting disputes over little provocation.
words.example: Grandpa grew quarrelsome after his second drink, contradicting everyone at the dinner table.
words.mnemonic: 'Quarrel' + '-some' (full of, like 'troublesome') = someone always full of quarrels.

words.definition: Strongly attacking or defending an opinion in a controversial dispute.
words.example: Her polemical essay tore into the new policy so fiercely that it sparked a week of angry rebuttals.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'polemos' = war; a polemical piece is verbal warfare, waging war with words on the page.

words.definition: To turn someone away so a close bond becomes distant or broken.
words.example: Years of unpaid loans slowly estranged the brothers, and now they no longer speak at all.
words.mnemonic: Make someone a 'stranger' again — to e-strange is to turn a loved one back into a stranger.

words.definition: To make someone feel isolated or unwelcome, losing their goodwill.
words.example: His constant bragging began to alienate his coworkers, who stopped inviting him to lunch.
words.mnemonic: Treat someone like an 'alien' — an outsider who doesn't belong — and you alienate them.

words.definition: To break or tear something apart into separate pieces, often violently.
words.example: The earthquake sundered the highway, leaving a gap too wide to cross.
words.mnemonic: 'Sun' + 'der' — picture the sun cracked in two and torn 'under'; from Old English 'sundor', meaning apart.

words.definition: A long, narrow crack or opening in rock or another hard surface.
words.example: A thin fissure ran down the cliff face, widening after every frost.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fish-your' — imagine dropping a line into a crack to 'fish your' lost coin out.

words.definition: A gap made in a barrier, or an act of breaking a rule or agreement.
words.example: Soldiers poured through the breach in the castle wall at dawn.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'beach' with an R — waves break through a sea wall and flood the beach.

words.definition: To cut off or divide something completely from the rest.
words.example: One clean stroke of the blade severed the mooring rope.
words.mnemonic: 'Sever' echoes 'severe' — a severe cut that splits things fully in two.

words.definition: Strong disagreement or conflict of opinion within a group.
words.example: Dissension among the board members delayed every decision for months.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (apart) + 'tension' — tension that pulls a group apart from inside.

words.definition: To irritate someone, or to rub against a surface with a harsh scraping sound.
words.example: His smug little laugh began to grate on everyone at the table.
words.mnemonic: A metal grate scraped by a shovel makes a sound that grates your nerves.

words.definition: To come into open conflict, or to be strongly incompatible.
words.example: Protesters clashed with riot police outside the courthouse.
words.mnemonic: Onomatopoeia — two cymbals go 'CLASH!' the instant they smash together.

words.definition: To make a dangerous or tense situation calmer and less threatening.
words.example: A well-timed joke helped defuse the argument before it turned ugly.
words.mnemonic: Pull the fuse out of a bomb — 'de-fuse' — and the danger is gone.

words.definition: A friendly understanding or informal agreement between nations or parties.
words.example: The two old rivals reached an entente that ended decades of border skirmishes.
words.mnemonic: French for 'understanding'; sounds like 'on tent' — two leaders shake hands inside one shared tent.

words.definition: A formal, official agreement, especially between a church and a government.
words.example: The pope and the emperor signed a concordat dividing their spheres of authority.
words.mnemonic: 'Concord' (harmony) + '-at' — a signed document that puts two powers into concord.

words.definition: A lack of agreement or harmony between people, sounds, or things.
words.example: There was a jarring discordance between his cheerful words and his grim face.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (not) + 'chord' — musical notes that refuse to form a chord.

words.definition: Peaceful in nature or intent; inclined to make or keep the peace.
words.example: She had such a pacific temperament that she rarely even raised her voice.
words.mnemonic: The Pacific Ocean was named for its calm waters; Latin 'pax' means peace.

words.definition: Cheerful and friendly, fond of good company and celebration.
words.example: The convivial host kept the whole table laughing until well past midnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' (with) + 'viv' (life, as in vivacious) — living it up together at a feast.

words.definition: Cruel and bitter criticism or expressions of hatred.
words.example: The critic's review was pure vitriol, attacking the author rather than the book.
words.mnemonic: Vitriol is an old name for sulfuric acid — picture words so acidic they burn skin.

words.definition: A general agreement reached by most members of a group.
words.example: After hours of debate, the committee finally arrived at a consensus.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-' (together) + 'sens' (sense/feel) — everyone ends up sensing the same thing.

words.definition: Causing strong disagreement that splits people into opposing, hostile groups.
words.example: The mayor's plan to demolish the old library proved so divisive that neighbors stopped speaking at town meetings.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'divide' inside it: something DIVIS-ive DIVIDES a crowd into warring camps.

words.definition: Involving destructive conflict between members of the same group.
words.example: The startup collapsed not from competition but from internecine feuds among its three cofounders.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'inter' (among) + 'necare' (to kill): killing AMONG your own — an internal 'nec' like a knife in the neck of your own side.

words.definition: To drive people toward two sharply opposed and extreme positions.
words.example: The documentary polarized viewers, who left the theater either cheering or storming out in disgust.
words.mnemonic: Think of a magnet's two POLES, north and south, pushing everything to opposite ends — no middle ground.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — harmony and discord
